query: For high-entropy-alloy multilayer protective coatings, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation? Specify what governs the behavior and why, an unspecified controlled comparison that would reveal it, the expected observations relative to a baseline, applicable boundaries, supporting evidence, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy-alloy multilayer protective coatings, the periodic interfaces act as barriers to stress-assisted dislocation climb and diffusion by promoting local solute segregation and mechanical mismatches, thereby significantly reducing time-dependent plastic deformation (creep) relative to homogeneous coatings.
generation.material_initial_state: A multilayer protective coating composed of high-entropy alloy (HEA) layers with alternating microstructural or compositional characteristics, each layer initially possessing a nano- or microcrystalline structure.
generation.intervention: A controlled comparison between a multilayer HEA protective coating and a homogeneous (single‐layer) HEA coating having the same overall chemical composition and thickness.
generation.conditions: Elevated temperature and sustained mechanical load conditions where diffusion-assisted creep processes are active (e.g., intermediate to high temperatures typical for protective coating applications).
generation.structural_mediator: The multilayer interfaces, which may feature local variations in phase, composition, and lattice parameters, create dislocation pinning points and regions of solute enrichment that locally slow lattice diffusion.
generation.mechanism: Under high temperature and load, time-dependent deformation (creep) in HEAs is generally governed by stress-assisted dislocation climb controlled by lattice diffusion. In multilayer coatings, the boundaries between layers interrupt dislocation motion and reduce effective diffusion paths, thereby increasing the energy barrier for dislocation climb and suppressing creep.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under identical high-temperature and loading conditions, the multilayer HEA coatings will exhibit a significantly lower creep strain rate (or accumulated plastic deformation over time) compared to homogeneous HEA coatings. Microstructural examinations (e.g., via TEM) would reveal reduced dislocation activity and limited diffusion phenomena at the interfaces.
generation.baseline: Homogeneous HEA coatings with the same overall composition and thickness that lack the engineered multilayer interfaces.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be effective only within the temperature and stress ranges where diffusion-assisted creep processes dominate. At extremely high temperatures or under loads that surpass the material’s stability limits, the beneficial interface effects may diminish or lead to coating failure.
generation.uncertainty: The detailed atomic-scale interactions at the multilayer interfaces, including possible variations in solute partitioning and the influence of residual stresses from processing, are not fully characterized. The magnitude of the creep rate reduction is also uncertain and may depend on processing parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of protective coatings: one set with a multilayer HEA structure and another set as a homogeneous HEA coating with identical overall composition and thickness. Subject both sets to identical elevated temperature and constant load conditions for a set duration. Use in situ high-temperature mechanical testing and post-deformation microstructural analysis (e.g., TEM and XRD) to observe dislocation behaviors and measure creep strain.
measurements: Time-dependent strain (creep curves) under constant load
Dislocation density and distribution at layer interfaces (via TEM)
Diffusion characteristics or evidence of solute segregation at interfaces (via spatially resolved spectroscopy)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the multilayer coatings do not show a statistically significant reduction in creep strain rate or if microstructural analysis reveals no impediment to dislocation motion at the interfaces compared to the homogeneous coatings, then the hypothesis that multilayer interfaces confer enhanced resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract This article presents the high temperature tensile and creep behaviors of a novel high entropy alloy (HEA). The microstructure of this HEA resembles that of advanced superalloys with a high entropy FCC matrix and L1 2 ordered precipitates, so it is also named as “high entropy superalloy (HESA)”. The tensile yield strengths of HESA surpass those of the reported HEAs from room temperature to elevated temperatures; furthermore, its creep resistance at 982 °C can be compared to those of some Ni-based superalloys. Analysis on experimental results indicate that HESA could be strengthened by the low stacking-fault energy of the matrix, high anti-phase boundary energy of the strengthening precipitate, and thermally stable microstructure. Positive misfit between FCC matrix and precipitate has yielded parallel raft microstructure during creep at 982 °C, and the creep curves of HESA were dominated by tertiary creep behavior. To the best of authors’ knowledge, this article is the first to present the elevated temperature tensile creep study on full scale specimens of a high entropy alloy, and the potential of HESA for high temperature structural application is discussed.

The tensile creep behavior of an equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloy was systematically investigated over an intermediate temperature range (500–600 °C) and applied stress (140–400 MPa). The alloy exhibited a stress-dependent transition from a low-stress region (LSR-region I) to a high-stress region (HSR-region II). The LSR was characterized by a stress exponent of 5 to 6 and an average activation energy of 268 kJ mol −1 , whereas the HSR showed much higher corresponding values of 8.9–14 and 380 kJ mol −1 . Microstructural examinations on the deformed samples revealed remarkable dynamic recrystallization at higher stress levels. Dislocation jogging and tangling configurations were frequently observed in LSR and HSR at 550 and 600 °C, respectively. Moreover, dynamic precipitates identified as M 23 C 6 or a Cr-rich σ phase were formed along grain boundaries in HSR. The diffusion-compensated strain rate versus modulus-compensated stress data analysis implied that the creep deformation in both stress regions was dominated by stress-assisted dislocation climb controlled by lattice diffusion.
